utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The next witness to be called will be Mr. Repinc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dragutin Repinc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, he appears as an expert witness. The expert report was filed early December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I believe it was on 18th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the 18th. And in view of the 30 days time-limit in Rule 94 bis, not all the parties have yet expressed their views, although the Cermak Defence has. The Cermak Defence, from what I understand, does not challenge the expertise or the relevance of the parts of the statement -- all or any parts of the statement under Rule 94 bis (B) and has expressed its wish to cross-examine the witness. Yesterday, I asked whether there would be any cross-examination by the Gotovina Defence. It was confirmed that there will be cross-examination, which the Chamber understands as an expression of the views under Rule 94 bis, under (B)(ii). May I also take it that could we understand the silence in relation to the qualifications of the witness and the relevance as there being no objections against the qualifications and the relevance of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we informally received a request that the Prosecution would start cross-examination only on next Monday. Could we understand the silence in relation to qualifications and relevance as there being no objections against those aspects of the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have filed objections this morning. A courtesy copy was sent around, and it has been e-filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I must apologise. I often do check my e-mail before coming to court. I have not done so this morning -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think a courtesy copy was just sent around. I get an indication that the Defence counsel have not received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, we have not received it yet. On behalf of the Gotovina Defence, neither I nor Mr. Misetic have received it, and we just checked our e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even if I do not read my e-mail, I'm usually briefed on any new developments by Chamber staff, and this was not part of it. Let me read it for a second. Yes. You do not, as I read -- the Prosecution hereby provides notice that it does not accept the expert report and wishes to cross-examine Professor Repinc. These are answers to the issues raised in Rule 94 bis (B)(i) and (ii). It, however, doesn't express any view on the qualification of the expert because a notice should contain a challenge of the qualifications or a challenge of the relevance. We do -- I do not find that in this notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution does not challenge the expertise of the witness, nor the relevance. We wish to examine him on certain aspects of his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that is now where -- it's clear now where we procedurally stand. And are you ready to call Mr. Repinc?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Markac Defence is calling Mr. General Dragutin Repinc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. May I then also take it that there will be no objection against the admission into evidence of the report itself, although you would not -- although you do not accept the contents of the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are not under Rule 92 ter, so it's presented as an expert report we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Repinc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration before you give testimony in this court, and the text is now handed out to you by Mr. Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Repinc. Please be seated. Mr. Repinc, the -- your expert report has been filed. You'll be first cross-examined -- examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is, as you certainly are aware of, is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First I would like to inform the Chamber and my learned colleagues that we are just checking, because we had some problem to enter the report into the e-court, and we are just now checking that this problem has been resolved. So in the meantime, with your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in the meantime we can proceed. Often expert reports are admitted into evidence at the end of the testimony, and there's nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. I will kindly ask you to state your first and last name for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Dragutin Repinc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honours, I would read a short summary in order to inform the public about Mr. Repinc's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not usually done with expert reports. However, if you would have a very short summary, I would not be opposed against it, because it serves the same purpose as reading a summary of a witness statement. So, therefore, if you keep it short, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Major General Dragutin Repinc is currently chief of the Administration for Planning at the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia, and he's in charge of combat planning of the forces, of programming, and making calculations, and for bilateral and multilateral military co-operation. During his military career, he completed the Land Forces Military Academy. He taught general tactics and engineering tactics. He was also adviser for operative war planning in the Zagreb Operations Zone. He completed the Command and General Staff School, and later on he worked as a tactics instructor at this school, where he also taught attendees combat unit deployment tactics up to brigade level, including decision-making and drafting of combat documents. He also co-operated with the US company MPRI, and he also held instruction in the field of organisation, management, and training. He also introduced the American Army training system to the Croatian Army. After he completed the American Command and General Staff course, he worked as chief of the Operative Planning Department in the Croatian Army, and at the same time he taught --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A short summary is -- giving all the details of the expert, if you would say -- yes, if you, please, could keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his expert report, General Repinc describes the specific role of Special Police of the Ministry of the Interior during the combat operations which were part of the Operation Storm, as well as during the operation of the search of the terrain that directly followed after the military and police operation. He also describes the manner and procedure of forming the joint forces of the Ministry of the Interior. He notes the specific role of the special police units, their organisational and operational structure, the relation they had with the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, and other units of the Croatian Army which were engaged in the Operation Storm. In his analysis, General Repinc chronologically describes and analyses the course of Operation Storm, in light of the engagement of the special police units of the Ministry of the Interior, the establishment of the joint forces of the special police units, as well as the operational and tactical tasks and duties during the course of the operation, and all this within the context of the combat operations. After the completion of Operation Storm, he describes the role of the units of the special police joint forces in the task of searching the terrain of recently-liberated areas, under the command of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. He notes the terminological differences, how the mopping-up operation and search of the terrain operations are defined from the aspect of the military and police duties, as well as the standard procedure for the implementation of the search of the terrain in liberated areas after Operation Storm. That was the summary, Mr. President, and now, if you allow me, I would move to the examination. In agreement with my learned friend from the Prosecutor's office, I was given allowance to ask some leading questions that relate to Mr. Repinc's CV and biography in order to be as expeditious as possible. If the Chamber agrees, I would begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Of course you'll understand that especially biographical details are not in need of any repetition. So if there is anything you would like to add to that, but otherwise we have a biography in the first chapter of the report, which is not in need of repetition. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, looking at your CV, we can see that you were educated in military schools, beginning with the Military Gymnasium, and then at the Land Forces Military Academy, and then further on by completing various courses as you have described. You have also described your duties in military units. My question is this: Until 1991, when you became a member of the Croatian Army, you were a member of the former Yugoslav People's Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, in connection with this, just one detail. During the existence of the former Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the system envisaged just one federal army, but what about the republics that were integral parts of Yugoslavia; did they have their own separate military units that would be under the management of each republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was Territorial Defence, which was under the jurisdiction of each republic. That is to say, each republic was in charge of organising, equipping, and training Territorial Defence, which existed for the needs of the defence of the whole federation, that is to say, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, as it was then called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, the Yugoslav People's Army, as the military system of the former Yugoslavia, was organised in what way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: What do you mean? In what sense? Organisationally? At its head was the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, and there were military areas which territorially covered the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time when the Yugoslav People's Army and the Federation still existed, was there any republican army, whether in the Republic of Croatia, or the Republic of Serbia, or any other republics that were members of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As I said, there was Territorial Defence, which had the duty of defending the republics, but also its duty was to defend the Federation, as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once the Republic of Croatia became independent and seceded from the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, did Croatia have its military component, that is to say, its own army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: At that moment, not anymore, because the Territorial Defence had been placed under the jurisdiction of the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened with the units of the Yugoslav People's Army which had been stationed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: These units, which had then been in that area, remained in the area. That is to say, they were active in accordance with the laws of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In September 1991, we became a member of the Croatian Army. Can you just briefly explain to us, how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, it was very simple. After everything that was happening in the Republic of Croatia, I decided to leave the former Yugoslav People's Army. I submitted a request to leave it. The request could not be realised, so I simply left the former army, and I joined the then Zagreb Corps which was operating in the area of the city of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And since that time, to this day, you have been a member of the Croatian Army and you performed various duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I can see from your CV, General, that from January 1995 until June 1996, you co-operated with the US firm MPRI. Please be so kind and briefly describe to us what kind of company is that and what sort of co-operation was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, MPRI is an American military advisory company which employs former members of the US Army, officers and non-commissioned officers, which offers its services on the market. These are services that relate to various fields, I would say various military areas, that these officers and non-commissioned officers were responsible for during their military careers in such a way that their knowledge and expertise and experience is something that they now provide to certain countries which wish to implement this if not fully, then at least to be acquainted with the basic elements of the manner in which certain areas are viewed within the US Army. And this is what we did from management of resources, training, managing personnel, and so on and so forth. So, actually, what this was about was that the company was supposed -- through Croatian officers, not directly, by addressing the Croatian troops, but through Croatian officers who worked in co-ordination with them, was supposed to pass on certain knowledge and experience into the Croatian military system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the MPRI firm was hired or, actually, who hired it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you all the details, but I know that an agreement was signed between the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and this company, according to which, at a point in late 1994, they entered the Republic of Croatia on the basis of that agreement and on the basis of certain elements that had been agreed on earlier, how and in what way this company would work and what it would do for the needs of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that experience, you also attended and completed the American Command and General Staff course, then you were the chief of the Operative Planning Department, and then you worked and you still work as a teacher and a lecturer in the War College. However, you also had another duty beginning in December 2005 until December 2007, when you were assigned the commander of the UN mission in Kashmir. Can you tell us, in a few sentences, what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: After I was elected to be head of the mission, that is to say, at the end of December 2005, I took over the role of what was, in fact, called commander, or chief military observer, in actual fact - that's the term that was used - with the task of the mission's remit, which means to monitor surveillance and reporting along the line between the Pakistani and Indian forces in the general area of Kashmir and all the tasks related to that; that is to say, this involved patrolling, gathering information, and conducting investigations, should there be any violations of the cease-fire agreement. Also, it involved sending out reports to the UN Command, co-operation with the Pakistani and Indian armies in that area, and all the other tasks that a mission of that kind involves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how many people did the UN mission number? How many people did you command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, the UNMOGIP mission was a relatively small one and had 124 persons, but it covered an extremely large area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're now going to move on to your expert report, itself, General. After the independence of the Republic of Croatia, and the Trial Chamber has heard much evidence about the armed conflicts that ensued, the aggression that ensued in the area, and Croatia, in a way, was faced before the establishment of its own republican army and, of course, the planning of that army. And I'm referring here to paragraph 23 of your expert report where you state that since 1991, in actual fact, before the civilian and military authorities, the imperative was to plan offensive operations to liberate the occupied territories. Now, can you please tell us something about those operations in greater detail, the planning operations that took place at the beginning of 1991 or, rather, October 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The establishment of the Croatian Army or National Guards Corps and the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, after the conflicts that occurred and after the part of the territory was occupied, it was quite normal that our prime task was to liberate those areas as soon as possible. And in view of that, the functions of the Main Staff were to plan the operations -- to plan operations which were intended to liberate those occupied territories in conformity with the circumstances that prevailed in 1991 and all the subsequent years; that is to say, looking at not only the military conditions and circumstances, but the political ones as well during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have document 3D00625 put up on our screens, please. It's a document that you quote, General, in your expert report, in footnote number 1, and it is an order from the chief of the Main Staff, dated the 15th of October, 1991. Your Honours, I omitted a technical detail. We provided the general with two binders containing the documents stipulated in the footnotes to his expert report in order to make it easier to go through all the documents, and we informed our learned friends of the Prosecution about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I spotted the binders, already, Mr. Mikulicic, clearly visible for the Chamber. There were two --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's not easy to -- not to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection against this very practical way of proceeding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, this is an order, as I said, from the chief of the Main Staff issued at that time. It was Colonel General Tus. The date is the 15th of October, 1991, and you quote it. Can you briefly tell us about that? May we have your comments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: What this order shows is that it relates to the liberation of the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia, which means that it was not exclusively linked to individual areas, but was comprehensive and issued instructions to all the operative zones that existed at that point in time. And the objective was, if I can put it that way, a radical one; that is to say, liberating these areas and reaching the borders of the recognised Republic of Croatia. And what is important in this order is that it stipulates the manner in which this operation must be conducted, which is that conditions must be created to introduce stronger forces, to route the enemy, to surround the enemy, without expanding into other areas and without mopping up the territory. So to reach the borders, surround the enemy troops, and - although it doesn't say so here, it is implied - once that is accomplished, then those enclaves which had been surrounded should be forced to surrender or would be destroyed one by one, depending on the situation. But what is important here is that there are no frontal onslaughts with enemy forces, which would slow down the tempo but lead to greater casualties. So that was what was stipulated in this order. And urgency was required. I'd also like to state that in this order, just as in a series of other orders that were issued at that time from the level of the Main Staff, the armed forces, in actual fact, were told that in organising an operation of this kind, they must organise participation and co-ordination with all the other elements which, in one way or another, armed or unarmed, contribute to the defence of the Republic of Croatia or, in this case, the liberation of the Republic of Croatia. And, therefore, in point 11 or, rather, point 12, the order sets out the responsibility to co-ordinate with the forces of the Ministry of the Interior. And since I know that this is something that was said all the time and repeated again and again, and it is defined in point 11, in item 11 of that order, that the manner of conduct by members of the armed forces, in conducting an operation of this kind, should be to prevent all abuse, all violence, looting, crimes, and everything else, and that this order should be implemented in a highly disciplined fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to tender this document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1913. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1913 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now may we have 3D00601, please, the next document. It is a document from 1992, a directive for implementing a strategic offensive by the Croatian Army. And the document is described in footnote number 4 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, following on from what you've already told us, that other orders followed, other documents followed on the same subject, we're now going to put this one to you, the directive from 1992, which once again was issued by the chief of the Main Staff at the time, General Anton Tus. To begin with, Mr. Repinc, could you just explain to us, in the professional military sense, what the term "directive" means, or, rather, "order"? What is the difference between an order and a directive, or the similarities between the two?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, in the final instance, there is no major difference or should not be. However, a directive is something that is issued from a top level of command and control, and, in fact, in the way it is written, it is -- the language used is freer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll read out the number of the document again. I apologise for interrupting. 3D00601 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I apologise if I interrupt you. Please continue, Mr. Repinc.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As I was saying, a directive is far more general and gives leeway to the commanders to whom it is issued to plan operations in their area of responsibility, whereas an order is a precise document, no ambiguity at all, and it must be implemented as the order was issued; that is to say, that all the tasks mentioned in the order must be carried out in the way stipulated by the order. Therefore, what I would say is this: The amount of leeway that the two allow a commander, a directive gives greater leeway to a commander because it is more general. But if there is a decision and if tasks have been set, as they have been in this particular case, then they must be carried out because an order, as a document, should have the force of law vis-à-vis those required to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, looking at this particular directive, whether you noticed any specific features which would be characteristic and important?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, this directive, just like the previous order that we saw, in fact, says the same. It is demanding that the entire Republic of Croatia territory be liberated. It stipulates the manner in which this should be done. It stipulates the manner in which the Main Staff and the resources that the Main Staff will use to support the operation zones in carrying out their tasks. And another thing that I'd like to mention is that in point 12 it defines that all attempts at brutality, violence, looting towards the population, should be prevented and that all the tasks should be carried out in a highly disciplined fashion, as befits the conduct of the armed force in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I have a number for this document, please Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1914. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1914 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have a 65 ter document. 3D00612 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And taking it in chronological order, you quote this document next in footnote number 6 of your expert report, and it is an annual order for training for the commands and units of the Croatian Army for 1994. So, first of all, we saw an order, then we looked at a directive, and now we're looking at an annual order, as it's called. Can you tell us what type of order this document is? What is this annual order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: With the arrival of General Bobetko as chief of the Main Staff, a lot of changes took place in the way in which the Main Staff functioned. And by certain plans that were devised, the Ministry of Defence or armed forces were directed towards the manner in which they should focus in their future preparations on military operations. And within that framework, annual reports began to be issued for training, and their prime goal was to determine the priorities in training for the military districts and for the various units. They were given a general remit and topic, and then that topic was a priority when the training courses were planned and implemented, when exercises and drills were held in the terrain, and when training plans and programmes were designed in military schools and all other courses designed to train the troops and educate them, so that a system would be set up whereby the units and the commands would be trained to plan their operations during that period of time and to create the necessary organisational prerequisites, material, and other training facilities so that when a decision is made to go forward into a major combat operation, the troops would be ready to carry a task out -- of that kind out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, if we were to look at point 2 of that document, which is on the following page both in the Croatian and in the English versions, we would see the following. It says: "The training of commands and units should be organised and implemented on the basis of training plans and programmes for the training of soldiers and units, focusing on the contents of the annual topic, the defence operation of the Croatian Army, and preparedness for a counter-attack." Now, could we have your comments to that portion of this order relating to the annual tasks or the topic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this particular topic, the important thing to note here is that the units were required to prepare themselves for defence operations, but not to stop there, not to stop at defence, but to move on to the next stage, which was that after a successful defence had been planned, a counter-attack should be planned, plans should be devised for counter-attacks for the military districts and for the implementation of their training programmes, which meant a counter-attack which was designed to resolve all the problems or, rather, to liberate the areas under their responsibility, and the guards brigades or smaller units to conduct counter-attacks as far as they were capable of doing within their remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I have a number for this document now, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document becomes Exhibit D1915. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1915 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us now look at the next document. That's 3D00613, and it's the annual order for 1995, which is mentioned under footnote 7 of your expert report. And I would ask if we could move on to the next page of this order, please, so that we could see items 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, we have seen in the previous document, under item 2, that the annual topic was the defence operation with a move to a counter-attack. And in this annual order for the year 1995 we can see that in item 1.2 is another annual topic which is called "Offensive Operation." As laymen, we can see that there is an evolution in the understanding of the use of the army, but I would ask you to provide an expert comment on this, if you can.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: During 1994, a great number of staff trainings were conducted, as well as various exercises in which members of the armed forces and members of the command were trained to be able to move from defence into attack. And through these trainings and exercise, this was confirmed, and obviously the chief of the Main Staff believed that we should move to the next stage, that is to say, begin to plan and implement an offensive operation for the liberation of the entire territory. This shift of focus from defence to attack showed first, in my view, that the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia had already been trained and were still being trained at the time to implement such a complex operation, but this also shows that evidently the conclusion was drawn that the issue of the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia would have to be resolved by an offensive operation aimed at liberating these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a number for this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document becomes Exhibit D1916. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1916 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, this Chamber has already heard evidence about the operations of the Croatian Army conducted in 1995; namely, Operations Flash and Storm even more so. Were these operations actually a continuation of the activities of the army in terms of the activities that were set out in these directives and annual orders, as we have seen them? How would you describe that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: It would be absurd to claim that all the plans and orders were made or issued in a context in which something was supposed to be done but nothing was really achieved. So looking back on everything that was being done, I believe that these were actually expert military and other preparations which were supposed to lead to the operations that were conducted during the year 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, now we shall focus on the role of the joint activities of the Croatian Army and police, which you describe in your expert report beginning at item 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for this purpose, I would ask if we could please see the document D1088.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: By way of introduction, you said what followed from the directive dating from 1991 and the later years that, for the needs of defence, members of the Ministry of the Interior would also be engaged. Here we see a document dating from the month of December 1991 which was issued by the deputy minister of the interior, Mr. Josko Moric, and which was sent personally to the chief of Croatian Army General Staff, Mr. Tus. And this is a report on engaging members of police administrations in combat operations. Can you tell us, from the expert military point of view, how did this actually operate, this co-ordination between the members of the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, policemen, on the one hand, and, on the other, the Ministry of Defence, that is to say, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia or the soldiers? How did this happen, and how was the co-ordination achieved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, we should perhaps start with the situation, how the special police units were established and for what reasons and why did it function as it did. As we have said, as there were no other legal bases in 1991 for establishing any elements that would focus on anti-terrorist activities and other defence tasks, the only thing that could be done and that was legitimate and based in law was to establish certain forces within the Ministry of the Interior which could react to the situation that arose after the month of August 1990; that is to say, after the rebellion of Serbs firstly in Knin and then in other areas. So even earlier, there was a so-called republic unit, the anti-terrorist unit Lucko, but that was the only force that was in charge of resolving hostage situations and establishing public law and order and carrying out anti-terrorist activities. There was also a part of the so-called special police units. However, only one of them in the city of Zagreb was active. And three others in Osijek, Rijeka, and Split were actually to be activated only as necessary if there were major problems as regards public law and order in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Around the 5th of August, 1995 [as interpreted], in accordance with the situation, the training of Croatian policemen was started. Around 90 members completed it. And in September, a certain number of them were selected to reinforce the anti-terrorist unit of Lucko, and special police units were also established in Rakici, Tuskanac, Crikvenica, and other places. So, first of all, as the colonel of the future Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia, of course, after an open conflict broke out, these forces could not respond to the needs because these forces were something that I would compare to the classical light infantry. They had infantry weapons and light anti-armoured weapons, and therefore these forces had no capability to oppose the armoured units of the former Yugoslav Army and the rebelled Serbs in the Republic of Croatia. And this is why the Law on the Interior was changed in the month of April 1995 [as interpreted] in order to provide the possibility to form the National Guards Corps, which happened later on, so that actually some of the personnel who had completed this training could now state whether they wanted still to be members of the Special Police or they wanted to join the National Guards Corps. And we can actually say that the Special Police was the basis of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia. So in that way, later on when the Law on Defence was changed in the month of September 1991, and the Main Staff was established as well as the National Guards Corps, that is to say, the Croatian Army, conditions were provided to establish all other units, because, as I said, without strong infantry and armoured units, without artillery units, without anti-aircraft defence units and all other units, it was absolutely impossible to wage war in the Republic of Croatia, so that what was happening in this period was that I would say there was a sort of transfer of responsibility, in a way, for the defence from the Special Police to the Croatian Army. And along these lines, as the special police units were also engaged in combat operations, such as liberating Pakrac and in Okucani, in the area of the Plitvice Lakes and other areas, it was logical that these units would continue to operate in the same manner but not independently anymore but, rather, together with the Croatian Army, which was chiefly responsible for the armed combat. And it was important how to define the mutual relations between the special police units and the armed forces, that is to say, the Main Staff. And what Mr. Moric, as the deputy minister, stated in this memo was that these relations should be, first of all, co-ordinated and there should be co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just for reference, you're referring to the document, the second page, section 4, that talks about mutual relations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Actually, the request was they should not command each other. However, it is also mentioned that when the police, at the request of the Command of the Croatian Army, is to be engaged in war operations, then the police units would be placed under the command of the Croatian Army, with the obligation of the Croatian Army to support, logistically and in every other way, the police unit which operates jointly with the military forces. And this actually means that once it was agreed from the level of the Main Staff and approved by the minister of the interior that special police units could be engaged in this manner, that at that moment the police units and, in particular, the special police units, became part of the combat forces which were engaged in combat operations, were placed under the Command of the Main Staff or any other command that had to conduct these operations. Something that also needs to be noted, however, is that what was insisted on and requested was that these units be engaged only in accordance with their combat capabilities and the remit of work for which they were trained and equipped and which was their responsibility at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just rise to my feet. There may be an error at page 22, line 23, with regard to the year, as well as page 23, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, you quoted and said that around the 5th of August, 1995, there was a training of Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: In 1990. Not 1995, but rather 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Repinc, at page 23, line 10, "April 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a change in the Law on the Interior, and you mentioned the month of April 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: 1991. I apologise. The Law on the Interior was changed in the month of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, the law was changed again, and this is why I would like us to see the document P1148, in which, actually, for the very first time, the notion of special police and the duties of special police were defined, which you quote in item 42 of your expert report, where you say that to fight against all forms of sabotage and terrorism, to prevent the abduction of persons and means of transport, free hostages, and perform other duties under the domain of the ministry under special conditions, that this is the only purpose for which the special police is established. However, as you already described, since 1991 the special police participated in combat operations. And here in item 45, you say that, actually, the first action which marked the beginning of intensive deployment of special police units in the area of Mount Velebit to the area from which Operation Storm was launched in 1995 was an operation called "Viper 1" or "Poskok 1," which began in late April and ended in late September 1992. Could you please tell us something about this action, Mr. Repinc, as well as something about the importance of the area of Mount Velebit, which was the area where special police units were active?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: I wish to note before that that it is true that the law actually mentions for the first time special police, as defined therein. However, as I said, as early as in 1990 or 1991, there was also the anti-terrorist unit Lucko as well as special police units, as they were called at the time. First they were called "Milicija" and then, later on, special police or police. And on the 15th of November, 1991, the then minister of the interior, Mr. Ivan Vekic, actually issued an order which established special police units in all police administrations. And the numbers were specified, how many members should there be in each police administration, and the number was around 100 to 150 members. And it was also defined that reserve units of special police should also be established with the same number of men. So the genesis originates at the time. In order to be able to operate and command these units, a Special Police Detachment was also established, but it was part of the ordinary police. And then, later on, beginning in 1993, a sector was also established, and it then changed. And with this law, it was defined that the special police was an integral part of the Ministry of the Interior and an independent element of the military and police forces of the Ministry of the Interior. As for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just to help the Trial Chamber out, you are referring to P527 or D527, which is the document on the internal setup of the Ministry of the Interior. And I believe that the Trial Chamber has already heard about that. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As far as the Viper 1 or Poskok 1 operation was concerned, it was launched from the level of the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, not from the level of the armed forces, and the object was to see that this very complex area be protected from infiltration by various sabotage units and groups, thus jeopardising the area and cutting off communication between Gracac, Gospic, and Karlobag, and to prevent these forces from endangering the Adriatic motorway under Mount Velebit. And I'd also like to say, and I think this is important in this context, that the fact that in 1992 the special police arrived at Velebit and remained there for the next three years certainly enabled them to become very well acquainted with the area and to function better in Operation Storm, particularly on the first and second days. However, on the other hand, I should like to say that it wasn't usual for the special police, which had its remit of operations, to be given a certain area to protect and defend for almost three years. That is something that the armed forces should be charged with doing and not the special police, especially as the tasks of the special police were determined. So where the need arose, they were, in fact, engaged and involved. But here we have a situation whereby the special police, in actual fact, entered the area and then for the next three years, deploying different combat tactics, it expanded the area so that at the beginning of Operation Storm they would move to implement the attack on those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in paragraphs 46 and 47 you refer to the operations which in 1993 were implemented and in which the special police was involved, but what I'd like to ask you now is for your comments on what you say in paragraph 48, the question of capacitating the troops through the civilian and police system of education and training conducted by the special police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: The special police, just like the armed forces, had to evolve by gaining greater knowledge and capabilities to carry out their tasks. And along those lines, after the first courses were completed and after the special police engaged intensively in combat operations, what happened was that there was a lull in their professional development, that is to say, the members of the special police's development and training, there was a pause. And they wanted to put this right by having the special police, who were already trained, training others, and also by sending individuals to attend courses which were organised in Croatia. I don't have the exact figures now, but I do know that the members were trained, and also members of the Special Police Sectors, for example, the Internal Control Department, was trained by authority of the Main Staff, and the sector was also called to attend extra training organised within the Main Staff for them to be able to carry out their duties and responsibilities within joint action in the operations. Now, the turning point took place, a major turning point, in the training in the Special Police Centre in Kofrcan, and there, at the initiative of the assistant minister, General Markac, this centre was to be established. The minister okayed it. And the centre devised certain plans and programmes for courses to be held there. As I say, those courses were approved. And in the course of 1995, two courses were organised for the leaders of the groups and units and for the commanders of the special units. About 135 of them attended those two-month courses. And at the courses they studied tactics, military tactics principally - that's the military part - but also police tactics which the special police applied principally within the frameworks of searching the terrain, mopping up the terrain after an operation. Now, what I want to say in this context is that if we look at the teaching plan and programme, it was implemented mostly at lower levels, that is to say, the level of squads, if you look at the military equivalent. And we know that during Operation Storm, for example, the special police functioned, I would say, almost -- well, not on a daily basis, but mostly during those days it was established within five battalions. But this kind of training was not implemented, and that is why the commanders leading these various units for operations at that level, their training was questionable because they were able to gain the kind of experience they needed exclusively through combat operations, whereas combat operations conducted by the military police were few and far between. Operation Flash was one, and then later on there was another at Maslenica and the Medak pocket, and their duration and the area over which they were conducted, and the forces that were deployed, were quite different to Operation Storm where, in terms of troop numbers and organisation and complexity, the complexity of the tasks themselves, it was something quite different, something that none of those people had, in fact, experienced beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the training of troops, with emphasis on military skills. However, during the training process, one of the subjects taught was relationships related to International War Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I would now like to have Exhibit 3D00905 exhibited, please. Document 3D00905.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, yourself, refer to that document in footnote 16 or paragraph 51 of your expert report, and it is a manual for conduct in combat stress situations. And on page 20 of that manual, we have reference to prohibited methods of behaviour and conduct. Could you tell us, please, General, how far the members of the special police were informed about International War Law through this manual?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to say because I did not take part in the training of those forces, so I can't say in what way the special police were informed about the subject. However, what I would like to say is that the Ministry of the Interior did issue this manual for the requirements of its members, and I assume that if the ministry took a step like that, then it also determined how the manual would be implemented during the training sessions and how it would be implemented generally in practice. In this regard, I'd like to say that within the frameworks of the training courses at Kofrcan that the special forces attended, within those training plans and programmes, within the frameworks of the theoretical topics which were taught for a period of 20 hours, they included topic 2, that is to say, International War Law, and from that I'm able to conclude that International War Law was studied at courses of this type.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there may be another error at page 30, line 6, in the interests of clarity of the record, a reference to military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, you said that later on combat operations were conducted by the military police, which -- as it says in the record. Did you actually say "military police" or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: If I said "military police," I misspoke, I made a mistake. I meant to say "Special Police," and I'm only speaking in referring to the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne, for being careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in paragraph 53 of your report, you speak of the strength of units, special police units. Can you just briefly explain to us how they were set up and what the strength of the units were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: In reading through all the various documents following the war and so on, the title of the units, themselves, and what the military equivalent would be to a unit of this type presents problems, even to the members who organise combat operations. So we refer to brigades, we speak about brigades, we speak about battalions, we speak about companies, and so on and so forth; however, this cannot be deduced from the organisation of the special police, itself, because within the police administrations we did not have a unit that would be called a special police platoon or a special police company, those terms. They were simply referred to as units, special police units or a special police unit. And depending on the Police Administration or Department, and I think that this was on the basis of the size of the Police Administration, itself, or the county concerned from which the special unit was organised, those units varied from 100 to 250 members. And in keeping with that type of organisation, a commander was at the head of each of those units, and then the rest of the component was organised by virtue of the number of members it had. This means that a unit that was smaller would have fewer instructors, fewer specialist training instructors, and so on. But something I did not include in my report is this: In principle, if you go from bottom to top, the number of special police members as classical soldiers, and then their leaders, the leaders of the specialist groups, which in military terms could be termed to be a squad, I would say that the ratio was 1:7, which means that one leader of a specialist group -- you had one leader to seven members of a special police group. Whether it was six or eight, that was also possible, but seven would be an average number. So above that you would have instructors, specialist training instructors, and then deputies -- commanders and deputy commanders. So a unit that had 100 members, the commander had 2 assistants or deputies; and at the level of a unit of 250 men, he would have 3 assistants or deputies. So, in organisational terms, the unit was organised in such a way as to have an equivalent number of instructors -- or, rather, for them to be able to conduct training within the unit, the necessary number of instructors, so -- and commanders to be able to command the individuals in the group. So this was how this was determined in organisational terms. But let me stress once again that when you had units of this kind and when you tried to organise them for a set purpose later on and line them up one beside the other, it was very difficult to say that two units, for example, would now be the equivalent of a company, or three units would be the equivalent of a battalion, or anything of that kind. What I want to mention here is, and I assume we'll come to that later on in due course, is that a unit, as a unit, per se, had a commander, it had assistants or deputies, and the situation was satisfactory for the classical tasks of a special police unit. But for greater operations, larger combat operations of greater intensity, when you lined up and conjoined these units and then had to command them, that's where the problem arose, because there would be a shortage of commanders for units of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, we will come to that topic in due course, General. Before the break, I'd just like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask for a number for the 65 ter document 3D00905, which is the manual titled "Combat Stress Behaviours" issued by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, before we enter into a new area - I'm looking at the clock, it's 10.30 - would this be an appropriate moment to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just would like to introduce this document into the evidence, and then we could take the break. So this is 3D00905.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1917. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1917 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to inform the parties that Judge Kinis, for urgent personal reasons, will not be able to sit the remainder of today's hearing, and that the remaining Judges, that is, Judge Gwaunza and myself, are satisfied that it's in the interests of justice to continue hearing the evidence of this expert witness, and, therefore, we order that the hearing of the case will continue. And we are well within the limits of the five days of Rule 15 bis, because Judge Kinis will be with us tomorrow again. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, before we continue, the Chamber has wondered several times during this first session to what extent sometimes the level of detail assisted the Chamber and to what extent there is some repetition; for example, the ratio of troops and those in command or those in leading groups. Clearly it appears in 53, and we spent time on that, which is mainly repetitious, and whether it's 1:6 or 1:6.3 or 1:7, to have that all explained in full detail, whereas a simple reference to the ratio which can be deducted from the report, anyhow, would certainly have done. Therefore, would you please keep this in mind in the continuation of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to find the proper balance on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us continue, Mr. Repinc. And now we will move to Chapter 6 of your expert report. These are the command relations within the Special Police of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia. Could we please see D527 on the screen. This is the Decree on the Internal Organisation and Manner of Work of the Ministry of Interior which you refer to in footnote 18. This Chamber has had the opportunity to see this decree on the organisation; but for the needs of your expert testimony, I would ask you to clarify paragraph 55, if you can, and that's the way in which Colonel General Mladen Markac, as the assistant minister who was in charge of special police, issued tasks to members of the special police in a situation when they were not engaged in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: The Special Police Unit was an integral part of the police administration of a certain county. Only the anti-terrorist unit Lucko was directly subordinated to the Sector of Special Police, which means that all the orders which were issued to the special police units to carry out specific tasks were not and could not be sent directly to the commander of the special unit, but only to the chief of the police administration within which this unit was, because this is the normal operation, that the person who is superior should know what is requested from his subordinates at every moment, so that all the documents which were drafted were sent and addressed personally to the chief of Police Administration, with a request that the document, whether it was an order or something else, be handed to the commander of the Special Police Unit. And in this way the chief of the Police Administration knew if his unit had received a task from the chief or deputy chief of the Special Police Sector to carry out certain tasks which were outside the Police Administration, itself, and outside of the remit of work and knowledge of that chief of Police Administration at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The situation was different when the so-called Joint Forces of Special Police were established. How did the chain of command operate in that situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: When the joint forces were established and the staff or the command of joint forces was established, once a special police unit from the Police Administration needed to become a part of joint forces, then the chain of command would go from the commander of the operation or action, through the chief of staff, down to the commanders of certain axes, and then further down to the commanders of the special units which were parts of these axes. That means that, actually, at a moment when a unit becomes a part of joint forces, then it is only commanded by the commander of the action or operation or the commander of the command of the joint forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the document 65 ter 3D00614. It is a document to which you refer in footnote 20 in your expert report. And for the needs of your expert opinion, you refer to Article 15, which reads: "The commander of the special unit is responsible for the work of the special unit police, to the chief of the Police Administration, and the chief of the Police Administration or, exceptionally, his deputy shall personally issue instruction for the performance of immediate tasks under the domain of the special police." Further on, you refer to Article 16, which reads: "Special police units are used according to the decision of the chief of the Police Administration, but if there is a need to use more than 50 per cent of the personnel of the Police Administration Special Unit for a period exceeding seven days, then the consent of the chief of the Special Police Sector shall be sought." This way of organising this from the proposed interim roles on the internal order of the Special Police Sector, does that correspond to what you concluded in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes. This means that if a special police unit is to be used to carry out tasks within the remit of its work within its police administration, then the chief of this police administration issues the orders to it. But if the task is to last more than seven days, and if the total number of members who are engaged in the task is more than 50 per cent, then, actually, the request for the engagement of this unit in such a way should be addressed for approval to the assistant minister for special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1918. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1918 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There are other situations in which General Markac did not command the special police units, and this is the situation to which you refer in paragraph 57 of your expert report. Could you please comment on this situation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, at the moment when it is concluded or decided that special police units would become an integral part of the forces which are conducting a certain operation, and they are under the command of the Main Staff, the chief of Main Staff may at that moment, if he deems it necessary, place a part of these special forces under his own command and actually command them directly or assign them to one of his subordinate commanders. So if the unit finds itself in such a situation, then it is not considered to be a part of the joint forces commanded by the Joint Forces Staff, but this is a unit which has been excluded and placed under the command -- either direct command of the chief of the Main Staff or the commander to whom the chief of the Main Staff assigns such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the sake of reference, this is the document D1094 to which you refer in footnote 21 of your expert report. Let us now look at a situation about which the Chamber has heard evidence, and that is the establishment of the Joint Forces Staff for the needs of a specific operation. I would ask you to comment on this establishment organisation from a military point of view.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Do you mean specifically in Operation Storm or generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As for Operation Storm, after the chief of Main Staff issued his order on the 21st of July that in the area of Sepurine a special police unit, 300 members strong, be sent there, on the basis of approval of the minister of the interior and on the basis of the order which the assistant minister, Mr. Markac, drafted, the Joint Forces Staff was established, and then it needed to make all the necessary preparations so that the joint forces could be organised and conduct the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. For the needs of your further evidence, I would ask for the document P554, if we could please see it on the screen. It is about the establishment of the Joint Forces Staff. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: This order was drafted in such a way that it was decided that the Joint Forces Staff would have a total of 15 members. Ten of them were from the Special Police Sector, whereas the other five members came directly from the special police units from specific police administrations. The staff, like any other military staff, should be organised in such a way so as to enable command and monitoring, the planning, organisation, and implementation of the operation for the purpose of which it was established, which means that actually it should be organised in such a way that it would cover the basic combat operational systems, that is to say, the combat arms and elements which are managed during the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you -- and excuse me for the interruption. In paragraph 60, you say that the Joint Forces Staff of the special police units of the Ministry of the Interior was not a military but a police command, and you say that the special police units were actually a police organisation and not a military one. So please have this on mind, and if you can comment on it at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I wanted to note that this way of organising the staff, in which the staff is organised and comprised not only the members of the sector but also included members from within the police administrations, shows that the sector does not actually have sufficient expertise to organise such a complex command and that specific persons working in police administrations were more capable of working in such staff than the persons working in the sector, and this is not a problem at all. However, a problem which did arise during the conducting of the operation was that some of the people from police administrations who were now members of the staff, because of the operational needs to direct the units during the operation, were withdrawn from the staff. I also wish to note that in the analysis which General Markac made after Operation Storm, he says that the forces which he commanded and which were engaged in Operation Storm were equivalent to two brigades, but they were only police ones, not military, because that was 2.200 men. They were engaged, and that would be one brigade. But what is important was that such an organisation was managed by only 15 persons who were supposed to be active, to work, to monitor, and command and control these forces around the clock. Another problem which arises when a staff like this is set up is what happened during the operation, and that was that this small head, as compared to a big body, was then further divided into two parts so that the staff, itself, was divided to the basic command post, which was in Seline, and the forward command post which was on Veliki Golic. So that even this number of 15 members which was reduced 3 persons who had left later on, so only 12 were left, was even further divided, so that General Markac was at the main command post, and Brigadier Sacic, as his deputy, was stationed at the forward command post on Veliki Golic. It is true that on the 5th [Realtime transcript read in error "15th"], in the afternoon, they linked up in Gracac. However, on the first two days, it was very difficult - and I'm only saying this from the military point of view - it was very difficult, with such a small number of people, to monitor everything and operate normally in such a way as to command the ongoing operations and plan the operations for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: An error again at page 41, line 25. It's with regard to the date. It says "on the 15th."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The record says --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 5th. I said "on the 5th."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us return to what I actually wanted to ask you, when you say that we should take into account that this was police rather than military organisation, when we are talking about joint forces, and when we say that the staff, as you say in your expert report, was actually a police rather than military command. What you just said, namely, the issue of the ratio of the number of commanders and the size of the unit, made you to draw such a conclusion, or are there any other elements that you wish to comment on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: I think that it's very important to know that it's very difficult to draw certain parallels between the military and the police organisation in this sense, because when one goes back again to these equivalents that we are talking about here, then one would see, for example, that the number of persons that actually worked -- well, we can compare that with the Guards Brigade or some other home guards unit in terms of organisation, the number of persons within the command that were part of this staff would be two to three times less compared to an equivalent similar organisation, if we could draw a parallel like that. But, again, I say it is very hard to make such comparisons, for the simple reason that the way in which joint forces are organised in compared to permanent structures of military forces are such that you cannot really make such a comparison. If we were just to look at the internal organisation of the staff, itself, then we would see -- I'm sorry, I don't see the bottom page. I don't see the bottom part of the page. No, no, it's like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, please allow me to intervene. When you're talking about the numbers, can we look at the part in your report which is in Article 68 or paragraph 68, where you say that it is evident with the strain under which the staff was operating, for example, compared to the Home Guards Regiment, which, according to the table of organisation, would approximately have the equal number of men in the operation as the members of the special police. So that Home Guard unit had 43 persons in its headquarters, while the Guards Brigade, which was larger and numbered almost 3.000 members, had as many as 56 members of the command. So then when you compare this to the command on the formation of the staff, which refers to 15 persons, then actually you can draw the conclusion that you are talking about. Do you agree with me on this point, Mr. Repinc?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes, but one would need to note that the organisation of the special police was somewhat simpler, especially when we're talking about the Home Guards Brigade, because it had more arms than that of the special police. But we could draw a parallel with the Home Guards Regiment, which had the same segments, more or less, plus engineers that also the special police had, but it was not so important and did not really participate in the actual operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one more issue regarding the joint forces of the special police. In paragraph 62 of your report, you say that the joint or the collective special police forces is a general term for the forces that performed the same task; and their size, composition, number of units, and how they were led depended on the specific situation or on the task that they were assigned, the enemy, the terrain, and so on and so forth. And then in paragraph 64, in the middle of the paragraph, you say after the completion of the assigned task, the task organised forces are disbanded and the troops return to their original organisations. General, did you find, when you were reviewing the documents, any data about the collective special police forces that were formed in that particular composition, for example, for the Operation Storm, had any kind of staff training or joint training, something that we would usually see in military units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I know that for Operation Flash a command was formed which was divided into two sectors. I didn't really review the Flash operation, but I am sure that General Markac was a commander there, that Brigadier Sacic was the chief of the staff, and perhaps some other persons who were on this list were also in that command. Perhaps I cannot be certain of that, but it's possible that they did have some joint experience from working together, especially because we're talking about an operation that didn't really last that long, and you couldn't really gather that much joint experience. But when we're talking about the organised -- forces organised for special purposes, in order for them to be able to function successfully and operate well, first of all, they need to be trained together in peacetime in order to create certain regular, routine relationships within the units that will comprise these special forces. I think we're talking about a sort of general term here. In this term -- in this form in which they were used in the Operation Storm, they didn't exist in that form before, which means that certain special police units which comprised the forces which attacked along specific axes, if not all of them, then definitely some of them never worked together and never met before, nor had joint commanders during those operations. Which means that during those routine relationships and mutual acquaintance between the commanders, and all of that was not something that was a feature in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. This is paragraph 65 from your expert report, where you talk about the problem that arises in such a structure. We can now move to the staff of those forces. And we see the order on the screen, and it is quoted in your footnote number 25. And we can see that the document is signed by the minister, Mr. Jarnjak - this is on page 2 - and also by Mr. Mladen Markac, as the assistant in the establishment of these joint forces. You are familiar with this document. And I would like to ask you, for purposes of clarification, to say how many members of the special police actually took part in those special forces during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As far as the staff itself is concerned, as it is stated in the order, it's 15 persons. As for the Storm operation, according to the analysis done by the assistant minister, in September there were about 2.200 members of the special police or an equivalent of two brigades who participated in the operation. These were police units from the 18th County plus members from the Lucko Anti-Terrorist Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at paragraph 70 of your report, where you talk about the situation when General Markac remained at the main command post. And already you said that the chief of the brigade, Sacic, was at the forward command post at Veliki Golic, and you said that this deployment was a result of the organisation of the communications of command and the relations between the -- or communication between the Main Staff of the Croatian forces and the Main Staff of the special forces because you could not really carry out this communication unless it was done this way. The Trial Chamber has already heard about the Rebus forces, but I would like you to explain to us, briefly, what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: This is a system which is a simple encryption system which functions between two computers, exclusively between two computers, which means that those two computers have the same encryption key. And when a certain text is entered, it can only be decoded with the use of the other key on the other side. So the police did not have this system. It was received for the purposes of the operation, and the encryption key was in the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff. Major Ricko, who was sent by the Main Staff or the Intelligence Administration - and this is also stated in the document - he was an intelligence analyst. However, during that operation, that was not his task. He was actually the person who was an administrator of this encryption system in the main command post in Seline, and this system, regardless of the fact that the command moved around -- and, actually, it did not move from Seline but was there throughout that whole period - and you can see that from the reports that were issued - with the help of this encryption system and which was sent on the 4th and the 5th, on the 6th and the 7th no reports were issued to the Main Staff.
