And then, again, on the 8th and 9th, reports were sent, and in all these reports that were sent with the Rebus system, the command post that is stated is Seline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Rebus system was the basic way of communications between the Joint Forces Command and the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Yes, it was supposed to be a protected communications system in order to dispatch basic documents such as reports and orders, but evidently in some parts actually it wasn't used, because had it been used, then General Markac would not be doing anything on the 6th and the 7th because there would be no way for him to receive orders from the chief of the Main Staff from D plus 1 and D plus 2, which means that some of those orders did arrive via other systems. I would perhaps say directly from specific persons from the Main Staff, sent to the Joint Forces Staff or General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 71 of your report is where you conclude that the process of command and control at the commencement of the operation, and partly later, was such that General Markac received orders from the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, transmitted them to the temporary command post where the staff, headed by Brigadier Sacic, analysed them, made decisions, and passed on the orders to commanders along the axis of attack. In your view, how did such organisation effectively function in the process of command and control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Since the organisation proceeded in the manner that I described, I came to these conclusions simply by reading all the analyses of the activities of the special units which was sent to the Special Police Sector. And when you read those reports, especially those that refer to Operation Storm, one can conclude that the commanders almost exclusively referred to the fact that the action commands or orders were received mostly from Brigadier Sacic. But regardless of whether they received them from Brigadier Sacic, the command structure still started from General Markac down. And Brigadier Sacic, even though it says that in the report, I never saw anywhere that he had such authority. But evidently this structure was something that was agreed upon, that was decided upon, and that Brigadier Sacic can, from his level, issue commands that had been agreed upon and co-ordinated with the orders issued from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Despite this -- or along this communications system, in paragraph 72 you also say that the communications system was also established by means of radio and wire communication. The Trial Chamber has already heard about the communications system of the special police forces, so I'm not going to dwell on that. Let us now move to the part of your report that deals with the question of the assessment of the situation before the Operation Storm was embarked on. You state -- you look at the enemy's doctrine, so can you please tell us something, General, about the enemy's doctrine, about the situation on the other side, in the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: What one needs to say, in view of the organisation of that army and those who were in command, is that the army exclusively applied the doctrine of the former Yugoslav Army, and, on that basis, they applied all the rules and instructions and documents referring to the use of military units in combat, in defence, or assault, which means that as far as the organisation was concerned, they used what they knew pursuant to what they learned and to their training and the manner in which they were organised and in the way it was laid down in those rules. So if there was a specific motorised brigade, it was organised precisely in the manner provided by the rules on motorised brigades, with all the specific points relating to replenishment, the specific characteristics of the terrain, and some other elements. What needs to be said, too, also, is that if, let's say, generally speaking -- if it was said that a brigade in defence was defending such and such an area, if it was possible, it would defend such and such an area. But if it was laid down that the command of the brigade between the first and the second echelon, this is what would be done. If it was provided for the artillery to be placed at one-third or two-thirds of the range, they would attempt to do that, if the terrain and other elements made it possible to deploy forces in such a way. In any case, the Army of the Serbian Krajina did not have any particular special characteristics in comparison to the classic organisation of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have document 3D00907, to which you refer in footnote number 38. And it is paragraph 78 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Here you say that according to the doctrinary theory applied by the opposite side, how the organisation of defence was set up and the emphasis placed on built-up settlements, and this is to be found on page 217 of this manual which in the Croatian text is 3D05-0767, and you quote it in your report, and this is what you say: "A populated area must be included in the system of defence. A brigade can defend one large and several smaller populated areas, and sometimes a part of a large populated area or town. Under all circumstances, the Territorial Defence forces and all the residents shall be involved in the defence of the populated area." Now, can you tell us something more about this doctrine of the defence of a populated area which was applied by the enemy side during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, when we're on the subject of this doctrine and the defence of populated areas, then the position was, as is written down in the brigade rules, that populated areas must be included in the defence system. That was obligatory. Which means that the populated areas, themselves, become - let me put it this way - the basis or fulcrum around which the defence is organised. Now, since the defence of populated areas is a very complex question, especially if we're dealing with larger populated areas, one needs to prepare such a populated area for defence purposes. And what is regulated by the doctrine or the rules is that in preparation for the defence, but in the defence itself, everybody is included; work organisations, the territorial defence, the civil protection, and the entire population or, rather, people living within that populated area. They're all included into the system of defence. And according to the other documents on the subject, we can see that this was a way in which, both in the directives and in the orders, it was expressly stated and ordered that populated areas be organised in that way so that they could be a basic focal point for the defence. And also the command posts of the units were also located in the largest populated areas. Now, when speaking of command posts, I should like to mention that similarly it was expressly required that the command posts be located next to logistics -- or a logistics company be attached to a command post, or a logistics company with all its basic elements; that is to say, the command and communications system, the support wings, and so on, which, in fact, led to the fact that should there be an attack launched against a populated area, it would be impossible not to target and not to act against these elements for the simple reason that this was the very basis of every defence system, to destroy the system of command and control and supervision and communications. And that would lead to a speedy collapse of the defence potentials and capabilities of the adversary. I'd just like to say that in the directive for defence, which was issued by General Mrksic, it says, for example, that the town of Knin must be prepared for a defence of this kind. And it even goes on to stipulate that for the defence of the town of Knin, a separate command be set up for the defence of the town, itself. Now, when we are talking about an area in which the special police was active, then I want to say that the 9th Motorised Brigade, as the strongest unit of the Lika Corps, and its command post was located in the town of Gracac, itself. But also I should like to mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, I apologise for interrupting, but we'll come to that. Let's take this step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that I'd like us to -- I'd like the 65 ter 3D00907 document to be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1919. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you would appreciate to have it admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was going too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I was doing is we have looked at -- how big is that document in its entirety? Because I always get a bit nervous if I see "Page 217" at the bottom of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is only a portion of the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that portion is how big, approximately? If it's just a couple of pages, I have no problems because then it gives, I take it, a proper context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As I can see, it's 18 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Eighteen pages. And we have looked at a very limited portion of it. There's no problem in admitting it into evidence, but in order to avoid that we are drowning in paper, I would like you to briefly discuss with Ms. Mahindaratne what is the relevant portion which you would agree gives sufficient context and sufficiently informs the Chamber about relevance matters and then to tender that portion. That could be this full 18 pages or less. I would not even suggest that it would be more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do that during the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, therefore, no final decision on admission is taken at this moment, and we'd like to hear from you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General Repinc, going back to what you were saying about the 9th Motorised Gracac Brigade, let's have a document pulled up for that. It is 3D00622, which is the document that you refer to in footnote number 39. It is an order for defence which was issued by the then commander of the Gracac Brigade, Colonel Jovo Kordic. Now, in your report, in paragraph 78, you quote part of that order, which reads as follows: "2. The 9th Motorised Brigade, shall, with the support of ready forces, conduct full mobilisation and organise defence in the area ..." And then it stipulates which area: "... with the task of relying on populated areas on the northern slopes of Mount Velebit." Now, General, may we have your comments on this order and the context in which you quoted it in your report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, in the report, we see defined -- well, following on from military logics, actually, the inclusion of populated areas within a defence operation is something that is quite normal. But what needs to be stated here is that if you do that, in that case - and this has already been said - that the necessary conditions must be created for the population in those areas to ensure that the population is protected, or, rather, that the necessary measures be taken that should the populated area come under attack, everything be organised to protect the population from the attacker. By organising populated areas -- or, rather, if you don't take into account the consequences that could arise from an attack is something that defenders must prevent. They must do everything to prevent the population being affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at paragraph 79 where you quote a second portion of that same order and where you say that a logistic company should be deployed to the area of Kruskovac and Gracac, a weapons ammunition depot within the compound of the metal processing plant and the Kruskovac Primary School, and a quarter-master depot within the RO MIG compound in Kruskovac Primary School, and the conclusion you draw from this, that according to this combat deployment, it is obvious that the weapons and ammunition depots were located in facilities within populated areas. You said a moment ago that it was in keeping with military doctrine and logics that populated areas be defended and that military units should, in fact, be located there. Now, from the aspects of a military unit launching an attack, on the attack, what dilemmas can arise in this regard and what could you do in a populated area involving a unit on the attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, I think there's this element which locates ammunition depots and weapons depots in populated areas, because the logistics capacities of the adversary units, whether in attack or defence, is something that can be called high-value targets because they are logistics bases for conducting combat and prevents the enemy. So placing depots of that kind within populated areas is something that demonstrates that, in actual fact, the security of the population is not taken into account, the population within populated areas, and especially so if depots of that kind are placed next to facilities or houses where people reside. And I have to say at this point that the Croatian Army, when it came to facilities of this kind, they did not put these depots in large towns such as Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a number for this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1920. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1920 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's move on now to the next paragraph, General, in which you talk about intelligence assessment made by the Internal Control Department, which the commanders of all the joint forces were informed of as of the 2nd of August, 1995. And for reference purposes, it is the intelligence assessment quoted in footnote number 49, which is already an exhibit, D549. What can you tell us about the enemy forces with respect to intelligence assessments, the adversaries to the special police units and their axes of attack, their communication from Gospic and Gracac, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the intelligence assessment is concerned, it is a fairly detailed one and speaks about the deployment of the 9th Motorised Brigade along -- in the various battalions, but it also refers to parts of the 4th Light Brigade which were to be found -- which actually belonged to the Knin Corps, but one of those battalions along the axes facing the repeater station Celavac were in that general area. What can be seen from this intelligence assessment is that it was assumed that if all the forces were engaged, all the forces that were in front, that in the infantry -- looking at the infantry, the advantage would be with the special police in the ratio of 1:3. But as far as heavy artillery was concerned, and especially armoured mechanised units were concerned, then the advantage was on the defender's side. And to this I would like to add, of course, the condition of the terrain on which the operation was taking place. And to this we need to add that the adversary in the area had been there for a long time and that in engineering terms it had seen to the area that was being attacked by the special police. And in that regard, if we were to follow on from military logic, it was questionable whether or not the special police could, in fact, route an adversary of that kind, an adversary that was in front of it, in the forefront. This could only be done by a resolute manoeuvre and an attack on a broad front, because by cutting off the defence line at any one of its points, the line would have been destroyed because the next line would be at a depth of six to ten kilometres. And breaking through any point along the line would leave the flanks and wings open to enemy attack. So they would have to pull out to avoid coming under siege, coming under a semi-encirclement, especially the portion on the left-hand side where the communications were cut off and facing Gospic, which is where our forces were located. On the other side, a break in communications -- in the communication line would still not have led to a collapse of the entire defence system if we look at the area towards Gracac, because in that particular area, on the right flank, there were no Croatian units which could lead to the same consequences as resulted on the left-hand side facing Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned, in paragraph 84, you refer to the importance of the terrain which was in the area of the attack of the special police joint forces. You said that it was relatively sparsely populated and very rugged terrain, and that that was one of the main reasons why the extremely difficult task of capturing that part of Velebit and its slopes towards Gracac and Medak were assigned to special units of the Ministry of the Interior who had spent more than three years in the area. In general terms, such terrain requires some additional preparation as compared to the, let me say, relatively usual military tasks. Can you tell us a few words about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, as for this issue, it needs to be said that this task of coming down from the slopes of Velebit into the valley, and also carrying out an attack along these hills towards Mali Alan and further towards Celavac and Prezid, only units or individuals who were exceptionally physically and mentally prepared to carry out something like that, to make such efforts, were able to do that in such a short time. So everything that the special police had been doing in the previous three years turned out to be decisive now in conducting an operation like this one, and that was precisely the reason why the special police was assigned this task, because frankly, perhaps, some guards brigades could have done something like that. But other units, the brigades of the Croatian Army and Home Guards Regiments, were certainly not capable of making such an effort, and they couldn't have carried out the task in the way that the special police did, especially during the short time in which this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 85 of your expert report, you talk about the center of gravity as regards the town of Knin. This Chamber has heard evidence that pointed to that. But I'm interested in the center of gravity in relation to the axis of activity of the joint forces, and you say that it was the town of Gracac. Can you please describe to us in several sentences the importance of Gracac in the context of the center of gravity that you talk about here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, looking at the geographical characteristics, we should say that Gracac was and still is in a specific area and that it's a very important communications hub, because the road towards Gospic leads from Gracac; the road towards Obrovac also leads from Gracac, and then it continues from Obrovac towards Benkovac; the road leading via Malovan to Otric and further on to Knin also leads from Gracac; and so does the road which leads via Bruvno to Udbine, which means that, in fact, the town, as a communications hub and as a town itself, is important because by taking it, all the movements that the enemy forces might make primarily along the front would simply be cut off and there would be no possibility for these forces to travel normally. The only direction which they would still have would be the one along the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, in the direction of Knin, if actually they wanted to find themselves in that area and to be exposed to the activities of the Split Military District. So, therefore, Gracac is important for this reason. Another reason is that as the 9th Motorised Brigade was there, in the situation in which the 9th Motorised Brigade left Gracac, then its communications system would be impaired and its ability to command and control all of its other units was, therefore, also impaired. Another important element needs to be mentioned, and that is that apart from Gracac, the other perhaps not such a center of gravity as Gracac but another very important place is the repeater -- the radio and relay hub of Celavac, and it was also the task of the special police to take over it, because, as I said, this was the nervous system, it was the hub of radio communications, also of electronic equipment, of listening to our own lines. It was the very hub. And at the moment when Celavac was taken, the whole communications system broke down, and that then increased the tempo of the collapse of the enemy's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 91 of your expert report, you talk about the zone of operations and the boundaries delineating it and the importance of the commander. Can you please comment on the issue of the zone of operations? I see that you also refer here to the NATO and US concept of tactical measures. And can you please relate this to special police, I mean, within the context of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: When one reads the documents which the Main Staff was sending to subordinate commanders, it is interesting to see, for example, the directives which were sent to the Split Military District and the Gospic Military District. And when the boundaries are mentioned, it says that the right boundary of the Gospic Military District was the border with the Split Military District and the other way around, even though the Main Staff was very well aware of that, that between these two military districts was the area where the special police was deployed, and the width of the area was around 18 kilometres. What should be noted is that an attacking unit can either be assigned a zone of operations or an axis of attack. However, the special police does not receive either of these, for example, if it said, Well, the special police should conduct an attack along the axis Velebit-Gracac, and, for instance, Lapac and Kulin Vakuf, or anything similar. What happened was that there was a problem which testified to the fact that either the Main Staff thought this not to be so important or couldn't define it; it did not determine the right and left boundaries for the special police in its order, which means that actually if there is no zone delineated by the boundaries, then there is no responsibility for the area which would be delineated by the boundaries. What is this all about? It is that a unit which is assigned a certain zone of operation or an axis of operation is, in fact, responsible for the area in the sense that it has to control the ground. It decides how the forces would be deployed within this area, but also how some other forces which might enter the area would be deployed and where they would carry out activities so as not to interfere with one's own units. Further on, if there is no zone of operations defined, then there is the problem with artillery and any other kind of fire within this area, and one could ask how to resolve certain problems that could arise if anyone used the systems to attack in an area where another unit was deployed at the time. And at this moment, I'm talking about the special forces. It is a fact that special police was not assigned a zone of operations, and in my view this also shows that special police did not have territorial responsibility for any area that might be left behind them after liberation. Of course, they were responsible for the areas where they were in at a specific moment and the axis along which they carry out an attack, but at the moment when they continue and move further, then at the moment behind them, if they don't wish to do that and have no sufficient forces for that, then they don't have to establish check-points; they don't have to leave other forces behind them; or do anything else which has to do with the monitoring of such an area. 2200 members of the special police -- that the special police as part of the joint forces had at its disposal, was an insufficient number of men in order to leave certain parts of these troops behind, because, in such case, the whole system would be broken down. And the question is whether there would be sufficient forces to reach the border. And the tasks which it did receive was to move forward and reach the internationally-recognised borders of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this context, I will ask you to comment on what you just said, and it's the question of the tempo of advance until achieving the final task, and that is reaching the internationally-recognised border of the Republic of Croatia from the initial point on Mount Velebit. So we're talking about a period of four to five days now. Can you comment on this sort of tempo and the area that the special police needed to pass through in this period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: I can only say that it was really a vast area, and what has to be noted is that the members of the special police passed along it on foot without the use of any combat vehicles or anything else. So great efforts needed to be made in this period. When we look at reports, it is evident that what I mentioned earlier, there were other problems as well; namely, the staff which operated as it did was also moving, just like the units themselves, and it had a very difficult task because the daily operations ended very late and they were to be continued the next morning, which means that moving the units, determining which forces would continue towards other axes, and also who would be the commanders who would direct the units, was a very complex process. And, likewise, at the command level, a process that certainly resulted in occasional misunderstandings, a lack of knowledge for the simple reason that if you are commanded by one commander, today he commands two units and the next day he commands with three other units, then, as we said earlier, we can hardly talk about continuity and routine relations. There was nothing like that. It just couldn't exist under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the eighth chapter of your expert report, and it's the time-line of the joint special police forces of the Ministry of the Interior and their participation in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber has now listened for the last, well, 15 to 20 minutes to a repetition of 90 per cent of paragraphs 84, 85, 91 to 97. There is no need to elicit from the witness the same evidence which we find already in the expert report. I have sent this message now a couple of times. Would you please take it seriously from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the introduction to this chapter, you talk about the difference between directives and orders, and in paragraph 101 you conclude that as General Markac received an order that had to do with the participation in Operation Storm, you conclude that he did not have the freedom in the planning process as, for example, the commanders of military districts, for example. On the basis of what did you draw this conclusion, General Repinc?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Very simple. The order which General Mladen Markac received is very explicit. It expressly states, task by task, what the special forces are to do in the first and second stages. And considering such a task, the only thing that General Markac needed to decide was how to organise his forces, how to set them up in order to achieve the tasks that he had received. And let me say that, once again, they were very strict, very precise, and one just could not do otherwise from the moment when the order was received on the 29th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am referring to two orders which are already in evidence. It's D535 and D536. Let us now look at another document which you mention in footnote 69, and that's the document 3D00541. This is an order dated July 1995 and issued by the assistant minister, Mladen Markac. And through the chief of the police administrations, the system that you've discussed already, it is sent to the commanders of the units of the special police, especially to the Internal Control Department. It is the order to dispatch reconnaissance operative units, numbering about 16 men, to the Logistics Base of the Special Police in Lugovo Sugarje. Can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: When the process was unleashed to send 30 specialists to Sepurine and the establishment of the Joint Forces Command, they obviously came to the conclusion that intelligence activities ought to be stepped up, in the sense of collecting additional information in addition to the ones that already existed, to the information that already existed. And it referred to direct contacts and enemy units up at the front-line in order to establish what their activities were and to find space between the two sides where the special forces could get through, and to place mines there, and to reduce the number of victims, and that once an attack is launched, that it could go through without being interrupted. So these forces used intelligence information to plot their operations. And the last report that I managed to find was a report from the internal control organs dated the 3rd of August. We know that the operation started on the 4th. After that date, I was not able to find anywhere any documents at all of an intelligence nature which the special police received from anybody, reports speaking about enemy forces or anything of that kind. And I find this rather curious that in the directives that were sent out to the military districts, that the Main Staff in those directives set out in detail - in point 1 of those directives - the Main Staff described the enemy facing those military districts or their areas of responsibility, although the military districts had their own intelligence organs dealing with matters of that kind and certainly knew the adversary much better than the special police did. However, in the order sent out by the chief to the special police, there's no reference to the enemy at all, so perhaps that was one of the reasons for which General Markac concluded that it was necessary to gather additional intelligence information to enable the attack to go through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we be given a number for 3D00541 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1921. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1921 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Mikulicic, would this be a suitable moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was just about to propose that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw you looking at the clock, so I tried to read your mind. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 1:00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But before I proceed, as it refers to the exhibit which was marked as D1919, it's 18 pages' document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I spoke, during the break, with Ms. Prashanthi, and she has no objections that I introduce the whole document into the evidence. This is 18 pages' document -- 18 pages including cover page document, and I think it's relevant in that portion. So I propose that the document in extent of 18 pages should be introduced into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, therefore, the way as it is up-loaded, D1919 is admitted into evidence. The main purpose was that everyone always considers carefully what is needed and what is superfluous. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the portion of your report dealing with the 4th of August. It's in paragraph -- chapter 8, paragraph 119 and onwards. And you say that according to the order, attacks by joint forces of the special police was organised or ordered in such a way that it determined the main line of attack or axis of attack and the auxiliary axis of attack. Can you comment on that, the axes of attacks by the special police and how they were organised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Well, I can comment the part which relates to the fulcrum and basis and main authority given to the special police, the line from which they were supposed to launch the attack. And since that line was a broad one, then the forces launching the attack have to attack along a broad axis, although military logics would dictate that a brigade, as a unit, if we take a brigade as being an equivalent of 220 men, that it would have a main axis of attack and perhaps two auxiliary axes. But here we see that we're dealing with four axes, and this was once again caused by the basic order given and the assignments given to the special police by the chief of the Main Staff. And the second point is one that I mentioned earlier on, and it is this: Since no strategic element of surprise could be achieved, tactical surprises could be achieved through the breadth of the axes precisely to make it impossible for the enemy to manoeuvre its forces along the communication line between Gracac and Gospic, and to concentrate his forces in the area of perhaps one or two axes of attack, which would make it more difficult to break through the line, much more difficult than with a broad attack over a line that was longer than 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, on the other hand, looking at this kind of setup, the following question arises, the control and command system. How was this organisation of attack with these four auxiliary axes reflected on the complex system of command and control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: If a system was functioning well in its entirety, then the number of axes or auxiliary axes should not represent a problem. But what was a problem, given this type of organisation, was the fact that at lower levels at each of the axes, a battalion command was established, looking at the strength of forces, but we saw that with regard to the establishment of the special police, that there were no elements from which that kind of command could be established. You had the commander, you had his deputies, but all of them, in principle, if I can put it that way, were infantrymen. There were no other forces, no other professionals who could command. And the second point that I would like to mention is this: In principle, when a battalion -- let's take a battalion. If a battalion was launching an attack, then it should have a command post and command from that command post. But here we have the following situation: The commanders of the various axes and their deputies, in principle, were at the same time commanders of the special units attacking in the area, which means that they have a dual role. They are there to command the entire axes and all the units there and at the same time command their own unit. So with respect to control and command, and the monitoring of everything, it makes things very difficult, especially because a commander of that type does not command from one stationary post, but follows his unit around, moving in front of him, which means that he has to traverse a certain distance and he has to command while moving, while on the move. And without the necessary structure to back him up, it makes it much more difficult for him to supervise the situation and monitor it. And faced with a situation of this kind, the number of pieces of information that that commander receives is vast. He receives all kinds of information; first of all, from the commander -- well, if he is a commander of a unit, himself, a special police unit attacking along that axis, he receives information and intelligence from his subordinate commanders who are, once again, subordinate to -- or, rather, have groups subordinate to them. Then he receives information from his deputy, who is in command somewhere else in another direction and on another axis, having the same number of men, and all this information has to be processed, dealt with, and then sent out to the Main Staff through one channel, and another channel at the disposal of the staff for receiving additional information, orders, and everything else, all the other elements coming in when you have combat afoot. Now, as I said earlier on, since there was not much experience gained, the special police only had three operations to go by, they didn't have more experience than that, so in my opinion the system was highly complex, they had a lot to deal with, and this placed a great burden on individuals who were in that kind of chain of command, particularly on the first and second days of Operation Storm, but later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the end of that first day of operations, that is to say, the 4th of August, in paragraph 126 you say that the greatest resistance came in the area of Mali Alan and towards Celavac, and that it was particularly important to cut off the communication line between Gospic and Gracac, which would make the adversary's manoeuvre impossible, and the forces of the 9th Motorised Brigade were separated into two parts, one defending the Gospic area and the other gravitating towards Gracac. Is there anything else you would like to add to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: No. That is precisely what happened on that first day. The special forces were successful. They managed to go down the slopes and cut across the communication line, which was especially important. So except for dividing the forces in two, cutting them in two, there was no longer the possibility of communicating and bringing in reinforcements. And as far as Mali Alan is concerned, this was a very specific area, complex terrain, which required very good planning and organisation for these elevated areas to be able to -- to take control of those elevated areas, and so the greatest losses were, in fact, in that area. And it was important, because having taken control of Mali Alan, the road was opened to bring in the other forces, to bring in reinforcements. They no longer had to take the roundabout road, but could arrive much faster using the direct route, which allowed us to continue our attacks towards Celavac - and I've told you of the importance of that - and then towards Prezid as well, which cut off the communication line between Obrovac and Gracac and, in that way, prevented the withdrawal of the enemy forces using that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 128, that's Chapter 8.2, activities on the 5th of August, 1995. That's the following day of Operation Storm. In paragraph 129, you talk about how the joint special police forces, not allowing the enemy to consolidate its ranks and set up a new defence line in the depth of territory, pressed the attack along the entire front-line and soon took the entire Gospic-Gracac road and the town of Gracac, itself. General, you already mentioned the importance of the town of Gracac and this road, but I would like to ask you now to comment on this part where you say that the task of the joint forces was not to allow the enemy to consolidate its ranks and set up a new defence line. And if you could comment on the fact that the forces of the 9th Motorised Brigade withdrew along the axis Gracac-Malovan, and they were still fighting against the special police forces which were advancing while they were retreating. So can you please comment on this advance which was aimed at not allowing the enemy to consolidate its ranks, and also the combat activities of the enemy who was retreating?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: As for the activities on the 5th of August, it was normal that once the road was cut off, that the forces which were still on the line should be pushed back as soon as possible and not be allowed, after retreating primarily towards Gracac, to consolidate their ranks along another defence line and continue putting up resistance, and it was possible to do this only if immediately the success was taken advantage of and if the enemy was pursued. It was facilitated also by the fact that the forces of the 9th Motorised Brigade were retreating but were not putting up significant resistance within the town of Gracac, itself, because had they done so, then the advance of the special police units would have been much slower than it actually was. However, it was also important that the resistance which these forces were putting up be prevented and that it not be allowed to them to stop and establish another line. It was important to continue to press these forces, as in the previous documents and directives which were sent by the chief of the Main Staff noted that in the area of Bruvno certain reserve forces could be stationed of battalion strength with an armoured platoon, which could then conduct some offensive operations from that place in order to try to recover the defence they had lost control of during these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After the liberation of Gracac - and I refer here to Exhibit P384 [sic] which is mentioned in footnote 87, that's a report on the combat disposition of the joint special police forces. So after the liberation of Gracac, around 11.30 or 12.00 on that day, the joint forces task, as you say in paragraph 136, moved from Seline and from the forward command post at Veli Golic to Gracac and became operational by 16 hours [as interpreted] in the Gracac Municipal Court building. You said earlier that the main command for the post remained in Seline, among other things, because of the functioning of the Rebus encryption system. But my question is as for the newly-established Main Command Staff in Gracac, how did this reflect on further activities of the special police forces, and why was it moved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: The movement was caused by a very logical reason, and that is that once the forces had descended from Mount Velebit, there was no reason whatsoever for the forward command post to remain where it had been until that point, because they could command from that area as well, considering the terrain. But as I said earlier, special police, as one could see during all these days, frequently moved its command post so that it would be as close to the forward line as possible, to the commanders, so that they would manage everything as easily as possible. By moving the command post to Gracac, this opened up the possibility to communicate more easily from Gracac and also to direct, manage, oversee the whole situation and see what would be the way in which the special forces would continue with their activities with the aim of liberating the entire territory. In addition to that, by having the command moved to Gracac, this also opened up communication, that is to say, the ability to link up later on, as Knin had already been liberated, to communicate more easily with Knin, on the one hand, and, on the other, with Gospic Military District Command, which was advancing in the direction of Udbine and the areas leading towards Donji Lapac and other places in that area at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the next day, and that was the 6th of August, 1995 - this is in paragraph 138 of your expert report - the chief of the Main Staff issued an order, the so-called D plus 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for reference of the Chamber, it's the document D552 to which you refer in footnote 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Some new orders were issued, including those to the special police. And further on in paragraph 144 of your report, you say that the special police units of the Ministry of the Interior continued with their advance in pursuit of the enemy along two main axes. One was Gracac-Bruvno, and the other was Gracac-Malovan-Otric. And you say that both roads were under control. I would ask you to provide the following comment: We can see from your expert report, and we have seen this in documents, that the task of the ordinary police was to cut off the roads and put them under control, beginning with the communications on Mount Velebit, itself, Prezid and Mali Alan, and then the road leading to Gracac, and then this road. How would you comment on these tasks of the special police which were, in a way, focused on cutting across or cutting off roads in the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: Cutting off roads was actually a consequence. I would say that this wasn't the main task. It just happened by the very fact that the area that we are talking about and the axes leading towards the border of the Republic of Croatia move along these lines. And the imperative was still, at the time, to reach the border as soon as possible. And considering the efforts which the units had already made by that point in time and their numbers, it was impossible to continue the attack in a frontal manner where, on a wide-ranging front, one would go and mop up everything ahead of these forces. But simply they advanced along the routes that would lead them as soon as possible to the borders of the Republic of Croatia. And, therefore, the special units, according to reports, almost exclusively moved along these roads together with the necessary security forces which were also moving alongside of them, both to the left and to the right, in order to prevent any sort of attacks or any ambushes, as the military logic would, of course, require them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 148, you say, quoting the document from footnote 98, that on the 6th of August the establishment of military police in Gracac began, and earlier you said that immediately upon the liberation of Gracac, you said that the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, had visited Gracac in the afternoon. And the situation when the civilian and military police entered Gracac, immediately upon its liberation, in your view, indicates what? After liberation, the civilian authorities are established, and so is the military police present. What does that indicate, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: That indicates precisely what I mentioned before; namely, that special police had its strict tasks which were connected to combat operations and focused on the enemy and not on the territory, as such, and, in particular, not on full control and monitoring of the territory, as this was the task assigned to the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, the ordinary police together with the military police. And the entry of these units into Gracac shows that they were doing their job in the appropriate manner. So once Gracac was taken over, that is to say, liberated on the 5th, already on the 6th the military police got there, and it organised firstly in Gracac and then along certain roads. It set up check-points and controlled what was happening in the area, as much as that was possible considering their numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see 3D00583 in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is the document to which you refer in footnote 98. It is a report on the implementation of tasks of the 71st Military Police Battalion, dated the 6th of August, 1995, from which we see that the military police actually assumed its obligations. It says here that the military police is active. Let us not analyse this document in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if we could move to page 4 of this document -- I apologise, page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We can see that reference is made there to the situation as regards crime and taking over prisoners of war. And under item 9 of this document, it is mentioned that around 10.00 a.m., one squad of OVP was sent to Gracac and the preparations to establish a platoon of military police in Gracac are underway, as are the preparations to set up platoons in Plitvice Lakes and in Donji Lapac. So, General, this is the document to which you referred; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would tender this document into evidence, so if a number could be assigned to it, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1922. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The next day, and this is one -- paragraph 149 of your testimony, is that on the 7th of August, 1995, and then in paragraph 150 you state that at 4.30 the temporary command post of the Collective Forces Staff in Bruvno became operational, and then you talk about how the collective special police forces began an attack in order to liberate Donji Lapac and reach the wider area of the state border. In paragraph 152, you talk about the friendly fire exposed -- that the special police forces were exposed to in Donji Lapac. We're not going to dwell on that. The Trial Chamber has already heard testimony about that incident. What I'm interested in is now this part of your analysis where you speak about the events after the liberation of Donji Lapac that have to do with the continued actions of the special police forces. And you talk about this in paragraph 155. Based on the documents that you've seen, can you comment whether the special police forces, after the liberation of Donji Lapac, stayed there or whether the joint forces moved further?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: According to the paths taken, the -- most of the -- the bulk of the forces stayed in Donji Lapac, and some of the forces went towards the other villages in that area in order to reach the River Una and the surrounding area in order to prevent a possible counter-attack and the arrival of forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the area that was supposed to be liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When we talked about the actions relating to the liberation of Lapac, Donji Lapac, and then followed by Gornji Lapac, I would now like us to look at the document that you refer to in footnote 102, and that is 3D00781. It's the war diary -- war log of the 9th Guards Brigade, which confirms the firing in the Lapac area. But you're saying that, actually, it was Gornji Lapac, and where it says that on the 7th of August, 1995, at 1330 hours, there were 130 shots fired from the town at the troops in Gornji Lapac. Can you please tell us how this friendly-fire incident occurred that the special police forces were subjected to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: I would like to say something about these different allegations. Reading both these things, I really cannot believe that General Markac, who was in Donji Lapac, mixed up Gornji and Donji Lapac, because if somebody fires at you from a multi-barrel launcher, you know where that fire comes from. So if there was some sort of mistake, it was probably made by an erroneous entry in the war log of the artillery of the 9th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I just wanted to be more specific. This is the text that we are referring to, and it can be seen on the second page in the e-court, the second page in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: But it's also possible that something else happened, and that is that there was fire both at Gornji and Donji Lapac and that the action on Donji Lapac was not entered into the war log. So I could say this, but it would be more speculation. I did read both. And reading both again, I say that I have more faith in the fact that General Markac correctly stated that he was fired at from Donji Lapac. Anyway, what I can say is that the actions that occurred that day and earlier, while the co-operation and co-ordination among the special police and the Split military zone was much better, and co-ordination with the Gospic military area was not as good, even though the chief of the Main Staff had asked for co-ordination of actions by the military police with both of the military areas. But in the war diary, also, of the Gospic area there is a reference where it is said that General Markac called the commander but did not manage to reach him, and so on and so forth. What actually this is about is again the situation that we mentioned earlier, and that is the absence of specific boundaries of action between different units, especially when the attacking forces are getting close to other forces and are merging with them. In such a situation, and when the operation is being planned, one had to establish a specific line where the fire support was delineated in the manner that the approaching units cannot fire below or above that line, particularly so that they would not threaten the units firing from different directions. It seems, on the basis of what happened, that this co-ordination was not carried out. It's evident that the information was not relayed about the forces of the special police being already in that area, and it also indicates that the area in which the special police was operating was also the same area where the Gospic forces were also acting without any boundaries being set, particularly because in the reports and plans drafted by the Gospic forces, it is said that they were going in the direction of Gornji Lapac, i.e., that they were moving in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Donji Lapac, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A correction: "Donji Lapac."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There could be another mistake at page 78, line 22, based on what the witness has said so far and the evidence so far. I'm referring to the words that he was fired at from Donji Lapac. His answer, starting from line 17 of page 78, is not consistent with that last line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a reference to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can verify that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what is being disputed here is this part of the interpretation where it says that you believe more the fact that General Markac correctly said that he was fired at from where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC
utterances.text: While he was in Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, what it says is that he was fired at from Donji Lapac. This was the difference. The second correction is -- and you corrected that yourself, when you said that it was actually Gornji Lapac and not Donji Lapac. This is on page 79, line 21, and this is corrected in line 23. I think that all of this is now clear. Now that we are making the corrections, I would like to correct page 72, line 15. I erroneously stated the exhibit number as P384. Instead, it should be P584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's corrected. Mr. Mikulicic, I have a few procedural matters which will not take long? But if this would be -- if there would be one or two questions you'd like to add, to do so, but otherwise we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could finish within two minutes just to show one more document on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I really need it not to be more than two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Or we could do it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would prefer --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better to do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to deal with a few procedural matters which will take me approximately two to three minutes. As far as the document which was tendered is concerned, that was 3D00781, the war diary, you wanted to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for reminding me, because it was my mistake not to ask for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1923. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And D1923 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Repinc, we'll finish for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, but I first would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you already have given today or whether it is testimony still to be given in the days to come. May I invite you to follow the Usher. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Procedural matters. A filing was received from the Republic of Croatia. I think any comment was due next Monday, and the Prosecution has asked for an extension of time, another week, from what I understand. The Chamber will, for the time being, not having seen the English translation of those submissions, will suspend any time-limit for response. And once we have seen what the content of it is, we'll then finally decide on whether or not we'll grant the extension of time the Prosecution has asked for, and also whether we'll grant it in its entirety or only for a more limited period of time. But we would like to look at the submissions first. That's one. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We would just -- whatever time extension is given to the Prosecution, we would ask for the same time, since under the original order that we were to simultaneously file our replies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At this moment, the time-limits are suspended until further notice, and most likely the Chamber, of course, will then grant extensions for all parties. Then the Chamber would like to put on the record that where it's granted the request from the Prosecution to further reply in relation to the issue of the appropriateness of taking interviews by persons who were not always at a long distance from the events which is the subject of the interview, that I think it was said that you would have an opportunity to orally make further -- briefly make further oral submissions. The Chamber noted that where initially the Chamber said that the Chamber might invite the parties for a second round, that even without such at that invitation second-round submissions were made, triggered more or less by a correction which was not really only a correction of the initial submission, the Chamber will consider all these submissions, invited or not, second-round submissions as well. So apart from giving a further opportunity to make oral submissions for 10 minutes, that it should be clear that even without an invitation, the Chamber will not ignore those submissions. Then I think, Mr. Misetic, that you would like to put on the record that where we have received an internal memo the 6th of January from head -- from Mr. Hepburn about the verification of an English translation of Exhibit D970, we received the memo, but from what I understand you would like to put on the record that you are not satisfied by the explanation or at least by the content of that memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. President. It's -- I'm told now that it is D970, but there is a duplicate in evidence which is P1205. We're not satisfied with the explanation. And it seems that there is a bit of artistry being used here by Mr. Hepburn, because he says that the term "artillery strike" is proper; however, in the context he believes there is a better interpretation. Quite honestly, Mr. President, we dispute that, particularly in the context of orders within a chain of command, where the lower-level order uses the same word as the superior order. We believe that for purposes of a criminal trial, where command responsibility is at issue, that the words should be translated the same, whatever translation should be used. But to take the same word in Croatian, translate it twice -- in two different ways in English, of course, fundamentally changes the nature of what is in the original documents. And in the context of this particular sentence, we believe it's more than just a minor issue, and we'd ask the Chamber to take further steps on the matter, including, if necessary, inviting Mr. Hepburn here to discuss the matter further. But I'd be happy to pursue the matter further in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The dissatisfaction is now on the record, and also the reasons for it. The Chamber will consider whether or not to further pursue and take the matter any further. Then we will adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 14th of January, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.
